# On the Strange Magic of Small Moments

I've been thinking lately about the moments that matter most, and how they're almost never the ones we plan for. They're the accidents, the interruptions, the things that weren't supposed to happen but did.

This morning, my neighbor's cat got stuck in our garden fence. Not badly stuck—just confused, the way cats get, having taken a route through the boards that made sense going in but seemed impossible coming out. I heard the yowling and found this orange tabby wedged in a way that suggested either great panic or profound laziness, possibly both. I sat on the ground—getting the knees of my jeans dirty without thinking about it, which felt significant somehow—and just talked to the cat for a while.

Not in a baby-voice way, though I probably slipped into that a little. But really talking. I told the cat about how I'd been stressed about work, about how I'd been meaning to do three different things this week and accomplished none of them, about how it's strange to be thirty-two and still not know if you're doing anything right. The cat stared at me with that ineffable feline expression that could mean anything from profound wisdom to complete indifference, and that ambiguity felt oddly comforting.

Eventually, I gently unstuck the cat—it required moving two fence boards, one of which I probably should have fixed six months ago—and it trotted away without so much as a backward glance. Typical. But I stayed there in the garden for another twenty minutes, just sitting, and something in me felt quieter.

That moment cost me nothing but time, solved nothing permanent, changed nothing measurable. Yet it's the thing I'll remember about this week. Not the presentation I gave (which went fine, I think), not the news I heard or the decisions I made, but sitting on the damp ground talking to a confused orange cat.

I wonder if this is what people mean when they talk about living in the moment, a phrase I've always found slightly annoying because it seems to suggest that you should somehow be *trying* to live in the moment, which immediately makes you not do that. But maybe it's not about trying. Maybe it's about noticing when the trying stops, when you're suddenly just *here*, in the middle of something small and unplanned.

There's a lot of pressure, I think, to make your life mean something big. To accomplish things, to build something, to leave a mark. Social media has turbocharged this anxiety into something almost unbearable. Everyone's supposed to be optimizing, building personal brands, turning their hobbies into side hustles, their experiences into content. There's this constant sense that if you're not doing something impressive, you're wasting your life.

But what if most of life is supposed to be wasted? Not wasted like it's disposable, but wasted like water running over stones—the water isn't trying to accomplish anything, isn't going anywhere in particular, and yet it's doing something profound just by flowing.

I've been rereading old journals lately, which I wouldn't recommend if you're trying to feel good about yourself, but I find them oddly grounding. The thing that strikes me is that my past self was always worried about different things than I am now, and was sure that reaching this current moment would solve them. And it did, somewhat, and then new worries arrived, fully formed, ready to move in and make themselves comfortable.

This suggests something both depressing and liberating: you're never going to arrive at a point where everything is figured out and you can finally relax. But you're also never trapped in any one problem forever. Everything keeps moving. The cat got unstuck. The moment passed. You get to have another one.

I've also been thinking about how we talk about time. We say we "spend" time like it's money, and we're always trying not to waste it. We're always counting down—how many weekends left in the year, how many working years left until retirement, how many summers left if you're lucky. This accounting-based language turns time into a resource to be optimized rather than experienced. What if we stopped thinking about it that way?

What if the point isn't to fill your life with big moments or impressive things, but to actually be present for the strange, small, real moments that show up uninvited? To notice the exact shade of blue in the sky today, which is different from yesterday's blue. To taste your food instead of just eating it. To look at people when they talk to you instead of planning what you're going to say next.

I realize I'm probably saying nothing new here. Mystics and philosophers have been on about this for thousands of years. But sometimes I think we need to remember it fresh, because the world is very good at making you forget.

Work is good for this, I think. Work is specifically designed to take your attention and hold it hostage. Also parenthood, if you have that, or caring for anyone. These things demand your presence whether you want to give it or not, and there's a strange relief in that. You can't think about the future when you're actually working, not really. You can only be in the task.

Maybe that's why people find meditation so difficult—our brains have been trained away from it. We're supposed to be planning, worrying, optimizing. Sitting quietly and just existing feels like shirking, like laziness, like a waste.

And yet here I am, a person who has accomplished some things, failed at other things, made some good choices and some catastrophically bad ones, and the moments I treasure most are almost entirely useless by any conventional measure. A conversation with a friend that solved nothing. An afternoon that had no purpose. A cat stuck in a fence. Sitting on the ground, dirty jeans, someone's voice I love in the other room, a dog sleeping in a sunbeam that will be gone by evening.

If I die in fifty years and look back, I won't be measuring my life in accomplishments. I'll be measuring it in moments like this. In the texture of specific days. In the precise feeling of being alive, right now, with all its strange weight and fragility.

The cat's probably fine, by the way. I saw it later, sleek and confident, judging someone in the yard next door. Already forgotten about me, already moved on.

I should try to be more like that.
